paragraphs: Resuming the subject of the last paper, I now ask whether the federal government or the State governments will have the advantage in winning the preference and support of the people. The two are appointed in different ways, but we must regard both as substantially dependent on the great body of the citizens of the United States. I take this to be true of the federal government and set it down here as a position, reserving the proofs for another place. The federal and State governments are in fact only different agents and trustees of the people, given different powers and designed for different purposes. The opponents of the Constitution seem to have lost sight of the people altogether when they reason on this subject. They appear to have viewed these different establishments not only as mutual rivals and enemies, but as free of any common superior in their efforts to usurp each other's authorities. These gentlemen must be reminded of their error here. They must be told that the ultimate authority, wherever the derivative authority may be found, resides in the people alone. Whether either government, or which of them, will manage to enlarge its sphere of jurisdiction at the expense of the other will not depend merely on how ambitious or skillful the governments are in comparison with each other. Truth, no less than decency, requires us to suppose that in every case the outcome will depend on the views and approval of their common constituents.

Many considerations, in addition to those I suggested on a former occasion, seem to put it beyond doubt that the people's first and most natural attachment will be to the governments of their own States. More individuals will expect to rise into the administration of these governments. More offices, with the pay attached to them, will flow from their gift. Their watchful care will regulate and provide for all the more domestic and personal interests of the people. The people will know their affairs more familiarly and in more detail. And a greater share of the people will have ties of personal acquaintance and friendship, and of family and party attachment, with their members. The popular bias may well be expected to lean most strongly toward these governments.

Experience says the same. The federal administration has so far been very defective compared with what may be hoped for under a better system. Yet during the war, and especially while the independent fund of paper-money issues was in credit, it had as much activity and importance as it can well have in any future circumstances. It was also engaged in a course of measures aimed at protecting everything dear to the people at large and winning everything they could desire. It was nevertheless invariably found, once the passing enthusiasm for the early Congresses was over, that the people's attention and attachment turned back to their own particular governments. The federal council was never the idol of popular favor. And the side usually taken, against proposed enlargements of its powers and importance, was that of the men who wished to build their own political consequence on their fellow citizens' prepossessions.

Suppose, then, that the people should in future become more biased toward the federal government than toward the State governments, as has been remarked elsewhere. The change could only result from such manifest and irresistible proofs of better administration as would overcome all their earlier inclinations. In that case the people surely ought not to be barred from giving most of their confidence where they find it most deserved. And even then the State governments would have little to fear, because, by the nature of things, federal power can be administered to advantage only within a certain sphere.
The remaining points on which I propose to compare the federal and State governments are how disposed, and how able, each will be to resist and frustrate the measures of the other.

It has already been proved that the members of the federal government will depend more on the members of the State governments than the latter will depend on the former. It has also appeared that the people, on whom both will depend, are more prepossessed in favor of the State governments than of the federal government. Insofar as each government's disposition toward the other may be influenced by these causes, the State governments clearly have the advantage. But from a separate and very important point of view, the advantage lies on the same side. The prepossessions the members themselves carry into the federal government will generally favor the States, whereas members of the State governments will rarely carry into the public councils a bias in favor of the general government. A local spirit will infallibly prevail much more among the members of Congress than a national spirit will prevail in the legislatures of the particular States. Everyone knows that a great proportion of the errors the State legislatures commit come from their members' willingness to sacrifice the comprehensive and permanent interest of the State to the particular and separate views of the counties or districts where they live. And if they do not broaden their policy enough to embrace the collective welfare of their own State, how can anyone imagine that they will make the aggregate prosperity of the Union, and the dignity and respectability of its government, the objects of their affections and deliberations? The State legislators are unlikely to attach themselves enough to national objects, and for the same reason the members of the federal legislature will be likely to attach themselves too much to local objects. The States will be to the members of Congress what counties and towns are to the members of the State legislatures. Measures will too often be decided by their probable effect, not on national prosperity and happiness, but on the prejudices, interests, and pursuits of the governments and people of the individual States. What has been the spirit that has generally marked the proceedings of Congress? Their journals, and the frank acknowledgments of those who have sat in that assembly, tell us that the members have far too often acted as partisans of their respective States rather than as impartial guardians of a common interest. For every occasion on which local considerations have been improperly sacrificed to the aggrandizement of the federal government, there have been a hundred on which the great interests of the nation have suffered from undue attention to the local prejudices, interests, and views of the particular States. By these reflections I do not mean to insinuate that the new federal government will fail to embrace a more enlarged plan of policy than the existing government has followed. Still less do I mean that its views will be as confined as those of the State legislatures. I mean only that it will share enough of the spirit of both to be disinclined to invade the rights of the individual States or the prerogatives of their governments. The motives of the State governments to increase their prerogatives by subtractions from the federal government will be overruled by no reciprocal predispositions in the members.

Suppose it were admitted, however, that the federal government may feel as much inclination as the State governments to extend its power beyond the due limits. The State governments would still have the advantage in the means of defeating such encroachments. Take an act of a particular State that is unfriendly to the national government but generally popular in that State, and does not too grossly violate the oaths of the State officers. It is executed at once and, of course, by means on the spot and dependent on the State alone. Opposition by the federal government, or interference by federal officers, would only inflame the zeal of every party on the side of the State. The evil could not be prevented or repaired, if at all, without means that must always be resorted to with reluctance and difficulty. On the other hand, suppose an unwarrantable measure of the federal government is unpopular in particular States, as would seldom fail to be the case. Or suppose even a warrantable measure is unpopular, as may sometimes happen. The means of opposing it are then powerful and at hand. The people's disquiet; their repugnance and, perhaps, refusal to cooperate with the officers of the Union; the frowns of the State's chief executive; the embarrassments created by legislative devices, which would often be added on such occasions: all of these would present difficulties in any State that are not to be despised. In a large State they would form very serious impediments. And where several adjoining States happened to be of one mind, they would present obstructions the federal government would hardly be willing to meet.

But ambitious encroachments by the federal government on the authority of the State governments would not raise opposition in a single State, or in a few States only. They would be signals of general alarm. Every government would take up the common cause. A correspondence would be opened. Plans of resistance would be concerted. One spirit would animate and guide the whole. In short, the same combinations would result from fear of a federal yoke as were produced by dread of a foreign one. And unless the projected innovations were voluntarily given up, the same appeal to a trial of force would be made in the one case as in the other. But what degree of madness could ever drive the federal government to such an extremity? In the contest with Great Britain, one part of the empire was set against the other. The more numerous part invaded the rights of the less numerous part. The attempt was unjust and unwise, but in theory it was not absolutely chimerical. But what would the contest be in the case we are supposing? Who would the parties be? A few representatives of the people would be set against the people themselves. Or rather, one set of representatives would be contending against thirteen sets of representatives, with the whole body of their common constituents on the side of the thirteen.

The only refuge left to those who prophesy the downfall of the State governments is the visionary supposition that the federal government may first build up a military force for the projects of ambition. The reasonings in these papers must have been employed to little purpose indeed if I must now disprove the reality of this danger. The people and the States would have to elect, for a long enough time, an unbroken succession of men ready to betray both. Throughout this time the traitors would have to pursue, uniformly and systematically, some fixed plan for extending the military establishment. And the governments and the people of the States would have to watch the gathering storm silently and patiently, and keep supplying the materials, until it was ready to burst on their own heads. To everyone this must seem more like the incoherent dreams of a delirious jealousy, or the misjudged exaggerations of a counterfeit zeal, than like the sober apprehensions of genuine patriotism. Extravagant as the supposition is, however, let it be made. Let a regular army fully equal to the resources of the country be formed, and let it be entirely at the devotion of the federal government. Even so, it would not be going too far to say that the State governments, with the people on their side, would be able to repel the danger. By the best computation, a standing army in any country cannot be raised above one hundredth part of the whole number of souls, or one twenty-fifth part of the number able to bear arms. In the United States that proportion would produce an army of no more than twenty-five or thirty thousand men. Against these would stand a militia of nearly half a million citizens with arms in their hands, officered by men chosen from among themselves, fighting for their common liberties, and united and led by governments that possess their affections and confidence. It may well be doubted whether a militia in such circumstances could ever be conquered by so small a proportion of regular troops. Those who know best how this country recently and successfully resisted the British arms will be the most inclined to deny the possibility. The Americans have the advantage of being armed, which they hold over the people of almost every other nation. Beyond that, there are the subordinate governments to which the people are attached and which appoint the militia officers. These form a barrier against the enterprises of ambition more insurmountable than any that a simple government of any form can offer. The several kingdoms of Europe carry their military establishments as far as the public resources will bear, and yet their governments are afraid to trust the people with arms. And it is not certain that, with arms alone, the people would fail to shake off their yokes. But suppose the people had the further advantages of local governments chosen by themselves, able to collect the national will and direct the national force, and of officers appointed out of the militia by these governments and attached both to them and to the militia. It may be affirmed with the greatest assurance that the throne of every tyranny in Europe would be quickly overturned in spite of the legions that surround it. Let us not insult the free and gallant citizens of America with the suspicion that they would be less able to defend the rights they actually possess than the debased subjects of arbitrary power would be to rescue theirs from their oppressors. Let us rather stop insulting them with the supposition that they can ever bring themselves to the necessity of making the experiment, through blind and tame submission to the long train of insidious measures that must precede and produce it.

The argument under this head can be put in a very short form, which appears altogether conclusive. Either the way the federal government is to be constructed will make it sufficiently dependent on the people, or it will not. On the first supposition, that dependence will restrain it from forming schemes obnoxious to its constituents. On the other, it will not have the confidence of the people, and its schemes of usurpation will be easily defeated by the State governments, which the people will support.

Adding up the considerations stated in this paper and the last, they seem to amount to the most convincing evidence that the powers proposed for the federal government are as little formidable to the powers reserved to the individual States as they are indispensably necessary to accomplish the purposes of the Union. And all the alarms that have been sounded about a meditated and consequent annihilation of the State governments must, on the most favorable interpretation, be put down to the chimerical fears of those who sounded them.
